metadata.title: AI chip sell-off overblown: Zero GPU slowdown after Anthropic essay, analyst says

content.text:
Investing.com -- The AI semiconductor sell-off triggered by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's essay on slowing AI capability development is a misreading of his actual message, with zero supply-chain evidence of any hardware pullback, according to Lynx Equities Strategies analyst KC Rajkumar.
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA), the dominant supplier of AI training GPUs and the most direct equity expression of AI infrastructure buildout, sits at the center of the debate, as investors weigh whether Amodei's public call for measured AI development signals a coming reduction in compute demand.
Rajkumar, who published a note titled 'AI Semis: Tempest in a teacup,' says the market's reaction is fundamentally mistaken. His supply-chain checks found no slowdown in GPU rollout, no cancellations in memory and flash, no cancellations at TSMC and OSAT companies, no changes to delivery schedules at semicap companies, and no disruption in the physical components ecosystem. That is a clean sweep across the entire hardware stack — from silicon to packaging — with no sign that Amodei's essay moved a single purchase order.
The analyst goes further, pointing to the essay itself as exculpatory evidence. "Nowhere in the Dario essay is there a call to slow down the pace of hardware roll-out," Rajkumar wrote. "In Dario's own words, 'pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress.'" He also argues that Anthropic has a direct financial incentive to keep compute capacity expanding: "We think halting technical progress and slowing the roll-out of compute capacity would impact revenue growth and the path to profitability. And that in turn might slow down Anthropic's march to IPO. Nothing in the Dario essay called for delaying Anthropic IPO."
On the real drivers of weakness in AI semiconductor names, Rajkumar is direct: "What is really playing on the AI semis sector is not the whimsical musings of AI industry leaders but macro-related headwinds coming from the 1) geopolitical sphere and the 2) the long bond." He identifies rising long-bond yields and geopolitical pressures — including ongoing US-China chip export control tensions and Taiwan-related risk — not any shift in AI industry sentiment, as the structural forces weighing on growth-sensitive semiconductor valuations. The distinction matters for positioning: if the sell-off is macro-driven rather than demand-driven, the investment thesis for AI infrastructure names remains intact.
For the near term, Rajkumar sees a potential reversal. "Ahead of the FOMC event, there could be a mini bounce in AI semis and hardware stocks from the Dario-related sell-off yesterday," he wrote. "Progress at AI semi names is less attuned to the Dario essay and more leveraged to whether the long bond yield flattens out, in our view." On the rate outlook, he added: "The hike this week and the promise of further hikes, if necessary, should hopefully mollify bond investors", suggesting that clear FOMC guidance, rather than a policy surprise, is the path to near-term stability in the sector. Lynx Equities characterized a quarter-point hike as already priced in at the time of the report.
